title: Hadith close
hook: a science built on honesty, memory and travel

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading hadith today, and your line: with a teacher. Did you ask someone, and what did they tell you? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

Every saying in this block arrived the same way. Aisha telling what the Prophet ﷺ did at home. Jibril asking about ihsan. Allah saying, whoever comes walking, I come running. Someone heard each one, held it, and handed it on, and someone else checked the one who handed it on. That's the whole block in a sentence. A science built on honesty, on memory, and on travel. Today the block on hadith comes to a close, and the question is simple: across all those hands, how did the chain hold? Today: hadith close.
screen: `HEARD, HELD, HANDED ON.` → `AND CHECKED.` → `HOW DID THE CHAIN HOLD?`

segments.voice: Walk back down the block, link by link. A hadith: a report of what the Prophet said, did or approved. Sunnah and hadith: the way, carried. Chain and text: who told whom. The text itself, because the words are tested too. Sound, good, weak: graded with care. Many chains. The science of men: who was he? Scholars on the road for a single report. Fabrications exposed, because they checked. Then the books: Bukhari's sound collection, Muslim's, the four Sunan that complete the six books, the early collections of Malik and Ahmad, and the four books of the Shia with their own science of grading. Then the sacred hadith, Jibril's questions, the women who taught the Sahih, memory, weak reports, the forties, commentary, and reading with a teacher. Three threads run through it. Honesty: the warnings against lying about the Prophet, taken seriously enough to build a whole craft of checking. Memory: words carried by heart, passed on just as they were heard. Travel: students crossing long distances to sit in front of one narrator. And one more thing the chain needed, which nobody could see from outside. Every link was a person who could have cut a corner, and the narrators the critics trusted were the ones who didn't. That's what the line means. The chain held. Not that every report is sound; this block spent whole days on weak and fabricated ones. What held was the method. Name your source. Test it. Say how sure you are. Tomorrow a new block begins: fiqh and the schools, what scholars built from the Qur'an and these reports.
screen: `LINK BY LINK, THE WHOLE BLOCK.` · `HONESTY, MEMORY, TRAVEL.` · `A PERSON AT EVERY LINK.` · `THE METHOD HELD.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank the transmitters. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one hadith from this block that stayed with you. Now walk back along its chain in your mind. The person or book you learned it from. The collector who checked it. The narrators before him, one by one. A companion who first heard it. You don't need their names. Just see the line of people, hand to hand. If you pray, you can ask mercy for them. If you don't, simply let some thanks go to each pair of hands. The bell holds the time.
Hadith close. The end of the block on hadith: a science of reports built on honesty, memory and travel, that kept the Prophet's words and checked them, link by link. Today's word.
Your line: the chain held. Today, thank one living link, someone who taught you something you still carry, and tell them so. Tomorrow: shari'ah and fiqh. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims often ask Allah's mercy for the scholars and narrators who carried the hadith, and students of hadith sometimes name their chain of teachers back to the Prophet when they teach.

fork.setup: a friend says: if some hadith are weak and some were made up, why trust any of them? what does this block answer?
options: trust the method: name the source, test it, say how sure you are.
fork.reveal: the scholars neither swallowed everything nor threw everything out. they graded what they carried, and the grading is the science.
